comm-systems-001.question: In wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM), which correctly describes how the transmission capacity of a single optical fiber is increased?
choices: One signal is split over several wavelengths sent at the same time, and the receiver adds them together to raise the received power and so the bit rate that can be sent above the noise
Separate signals are placed on laser beams of different frequencies, combined into one fiber, and separated by wavelength at the receiver
Light at a single wavelength is divided finely in time, and several signals are packed into it in turn, multiplexing them without adding wavelengths
comm-systems-001.explanation: WDM relies on the fact that light at different frequencies propagates through a linear medium without affecting each other, and places an independent signal on each wavelength. A multiplexer combines them into one fiber, and at the receiver a demultiplexer such as thin-film filters or an arrayed waveguide grating separates them by wavelength for separate detection, so the capacity is roughly the bit rate per wavelength times the number of wavelengths. Sending the same signal on several wavelengths only divides the power and does not raise capacity. Packing signals in time slots is time-division multiplexing (TDM), a different kind of multiplexing used within one wavelength. Real systems combine the two.

comm-systems-002.question: Near a wavelength of 1550 nm, WDM channels are placed at a frequency spacing of 50 GHz. Which is closest to this spacing expressed in wavelength? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
choices: About 0.4 nm
About 0.8 nm
About 0.04 nm
comm-systems-002.explanation: Frequency spacing converts to wavelength spacing as Δλ = λ²Δf/c. Δλ = (1550×10⁻⁹)² × 50×10⁹ / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 4.0×10⁻¹⁰ m, or about 0.4 nm. About 0.8 nm is the value for a 100 GHz spacing; it is easy to confuse because 100 GHz corresponds to roughly 0.8 nm near 1550 nm. About 0.04 nm is an order-of-magnitude error. WDM channels are normally placed at equal frequency intervals, and since the wavelength spacing is proportional to λ², it becomes slightly narrower toward shorter wavelengths.

comm-systems-003.question: Why did the EDFA make WDM transmission with many wavelengths practical?
choices: It demultiplexes and detects each channel, reshapes the waveform electrically and retransmits it (regenerative repeating), so no noise accumulates at all along the link
It selects and boosts only one wavelength, so crosstalk and four-wave-mixing light from neighboring channels are removed
A single unit amplifies the many channels within its gain band of tens of nm in the 1.55 µm region at once, without converting them back to electrical signals
comm-systems-003.explanation: An EDFA amplifies light as light, through stimulated emission from population-inverted erbium ions. Its gain spans tens of nm centered on the C band (about 1530–1565 nm) in the 1.55 µm region, so one unit can amplify well over tens of channels at once, independent of the signal bit rate and modulation format. Demultiplexing, reshaping electrically and retransmitting is how regenerative repeaters worked before EDFAs; they needed a receiver and transmitter for every channel, which made scaling WDM difficult. An EDFA also amplifies spontaneous emission (ASE), so noise does accumulate at each repeater. It is not a device that picks out and amplifies just one wavelength.

comm-systems-004.question: In long-haul WDM transmission with many cascaded EDFAs, what is the main purpose of inserting a gain-flattening filter (GFF)?
choices: To remove only the pump wavelength (980 nm or 1480 nm) so that the EDFA pump light does not reach the receiver along with the signal and add noise
The EDFA gain varies with wavelength, and per-channel differences in power and OSNR add up over many stages, so the filter cancels them to equalize the channels
To remove unwanted frequency components between channels so that the spacing to neighboring channels can be narrowed and more channels can be packed into the same amplifier band
comm-systems-004.explanation: The EDFA gain spectrum is not flat: it has a sharp peak near 1530 nm and is gentler on the long-wavelength side. Even a small difference per stage adds up; for example, a 1 dB difference over 10 stages becomes 10 dB, so low-gain channels run short of OSNR while high-gain channels suffer more from nonlinearity. A filter whose loss spectrum is the inverse of the gain shape is therefore built into the amplifier to equalize the gain of all channels. Separating or combining pump and signal is the job of the wavelength-multiplexing coupler, not the purpose of a GFF. Channel spacing is set by the transmitter frequencies and the characteristics of the multiplexers and demultiplexers.

comm-systems-005.question: An optical link has a transmitter output of 0 dBm and a receiver sensitivity of −24 dBm. Connector losses total 1 dB, a system margin of 3 dB is reserved, and the fiber loss (including fusion splices) is 0.25 dB/km. Which is closest to the maximum transmission distance set by loss?
choices: About 92 km
About 96 km
About 80 km
comm-systems-005.explanation: The loss budget (power budget) is the difference between transmitter output and receiver sensitivity, 0 − (−24) = 24 dB. Subtracting the 1 dB of connectors and a 3 dB margin for component aging, temperature changes and repair splices leaves 24 − 1 − 3 = 20 dB for the fiber, so the distance is 20 / 0.25 = 80 km. About 92 km forgets to subtract the margin, and about 96 km ignores every loss other than the fiber. In real designs the budget also includes the extra received power needed to keep the same error rate in the presence of chromatic dispersion and other impairments (the power penalty), and the distance is chosen to satisfy both the loss and the dispersion conditions.

comm-systems-006.question: The accumulated dispersion of 80 km of single-mode fiber with a chromatic dispersion of 17 ps/(nm·km) is to be cancelled exactly with dispersion-compensating fiber (DCF) of −100 ps/(nm·km). Which is closest to the required DCF length?
choices: About 13.6 km
About 80 km
About 1.36 km
comm-systems-006.explanation: The accumulated dispersion of the link is 17 × 80 = 1360 ps/nm. With a DCF length L, −100 × L = −1360 ps/nm gives L = 13.6 km. About 80 km assumes the same length as the link is needed and ignores the ratio of the dispersion magnitudes. About 1.36 km is an order-of-magnitude error. DCF has higher loss than ordinary fiber (at 0.5 dB/km, for example, 13.6 km adds about 6.8 dB), and its small core makes nonlinearity more likely, so it was commonly placed between the stages of a two-stage EDFA. In transmission with coherent detection, dispersion is compensated by digital signal processing at the receiver, so configurations without DCF are also possible.

comm-systems-007.question: Keeping the same symbol rate, a link changes from binary intensity modulation (NRZ) to four-level intensity modulation (PAM4). Which correctly describes the change? (The range between minimum and maximum optical intensity is the same.)
choices: Four levels are used, so each symbol carries 4 bits and the bit rate becomes four times higher, with the required SNR unchanged
The bit rate doubles and the spectral width also doubles, so a wider-band receiver is needed, while the required SNR goes down
Each symbol carries 2 bits, so the bit rate doubles, but the level spacing drops to 1/3, so a higher SNR is needed for the same error rate
comm-systems-007.explanation: PAM4 uses four intensity levels and sends log₂4 = 2 bits per symbol, so at the same symbol rate the bit rate doubles. Fitting four levels into the same intensity range splits it into three gaps, each 1/3 of the NRZ spacing, so errors become more likely for the same noise. In terms of the electrical SNR of the received signal this is a penalty of 20 log₁₀3 ≈ 9.5 dB; when thermal noise dominates, the received optical power must be raised by about 4.8 dB (10 log₁₀3). The number of bits doubles; it does not quadruple. The spectral width is set mainly by the symbol rate, so at the same symbol rate it does not grow, and the advantage of PAM4 is that the bit rate can be raised while keeping bandwidth-limited components.

comm-systems-008.question: When dispersion-shifted fiber with nearly zero chromatic dispersion near 1550 nm is used for WDM transmission, problems between channels are likely. What is the main cause?
choices: Without dispersion the effect of birefringence is not cancelled, so polarization-mode dispersion grows and the delay of each channel varies, causing intersymbol interference
Without dispersion the channels stay in phase as they propagate, so four-wave mixing occurs efficiently and the generated light falls on other channels as crosstalk
Without dispersion the pulses do not spread and keep a high peak power, so they exceed the stimulated Brillouin scattering threshold and all channels are reflected back toward the input
comm-systems-008.explanation: Four-wave mixing (FWM) is the process by which third-order nonlinearity generates light at f_i + f_j − f_k from light at frequencies f_i, f_j and f_k. Its efficiency is set by phase matching between the channels: large chromatic dispersion quickly destroys the phase relationship and weakens it, but with nearly zero dispersion it stays well matched and FWM is strong. With equally spaced channels, the generated light lands exactly on other channel frequencies and becomes crosstalk that cannot be removed. This is why non-zero dispersion-shifted fiber, which leaves a small dispersion at 1550 nm, is used. Polarization-mode dispersion is set by fiber birefringence, a property separate from the size of chromatic dispersion. Stimulated Brillouin scattering is backscattering caused by strong narrow-linewidth light and is not determined by whether dispersion is present.

comm-systems-009.question: For a link of N identical spans, the OSNR measured in a 0.1 nm noise bandwidth can be estimated as OSNR[dB] ≈ 58 + P_ch − L_span − NF − 10 log₁₀N (P_ch is the input power per channel [dBm], L_span the span loss [dB], NF the EDFA noise figure [dB]). With P_ch = 0 dBm, L_span = 22 dB, NF = 5 dB and N = 10, which is closest to the OSNR?
choices: About 21 dB
About 31 dB
About 11 dB
comm-systems-009.explanation: Substituting gives 58 + 0 − 22 − 5 − 10 log₁₀10 = 58 − 22 − 5 − 10 = 21 dB. The constant 58 comes from the product of the photon energy at 1550 nm, hν ≈ 1.28×10⁻¹⁹ J, and the reference bandwidth of 12.5 GHz (0.1 nm), which is about −58 dBm. Each EDFA adds the same amount of ASE noise, so the noise power is proportional to the number of spans and the OSNR falls by 10 log₁₀N. About 31 dB forgets the degradation from the number of spans, and about 11 dB subtracts it twice as 20 log₁₀N. The required OSNR is set by the modulation format and error correction; if it is not met, raise the input power or shorten the spans.

comm-systems-010.question: A 1200 km link with a loss of 0.2 dB/km is built either with EDFAs every 60 km (20 spans) or every 120 km (10 spans). Using the estimate OSNR[dB] ≈ 58 + P_ch − L_span − NF − 10 log₁₀N, with the same input power and NF, which correctly describes the difference in OSNR?
choices: The 120 km spacing is about 3 dB higher
The 60 km spacing is about 9 dB higher
Both have the same total loss of 240 dB, so they are equal
comm-systems-010.explanation: A 60 km span has 12 dB of loss with 20 stages, and a 120 km span has 24 dB with 10 stages. The OSNR difference is (−12 − 10 log₁₀20) − (−24 − 10 log₁₀10) = (−12 − 13.0) − (−34) ≈ 9 dB, so the 60 km spacing is about 9 dB higher. Span loss counts directly in dB while the number of stages counts only as 10 log₁₀N, so shorter spans win. Saying the 120 km spacing is better looks only at the halved number of amplifiers acting as noise sources, a gain of about 3 dB, and overlooks that each amplifier must make up 12 dB (about 16 times) more loss. Even with the same total loss, noise is added at each amplifier in proportion to its gain, so the two are not equal.

comm-systems-011.question: Which is closest to the line bit rate (including error-correction overhead) when dual-polarization 16QAM (DP-16QAM) is sent at a symbol rate of 32 GBd?
choices: About 256 Gb/s
About 128 Gb/s
About 1024 Gb/s
comm-systems-011.explanation: 16QAM uses 16 constellation points formed by combinations of amplitude and phase, so each symbol carries log₂16 = 4 bits. Polarization multiplexing, which places separate signals on two orthogonal polarizations, doubles this again: 4 × 2 × 32 GBd = 256 Gb/s. About 128 Gb/s forgets the factor of 2 from polarization multiplexing, and about 1024 Gb/s mistakenly multiplies by the 16 points as if they were bits. The net data rate actually carried is this value minus the error-correction overhead, so this example corresponds to 200 Gb/s-class transmission.

comm-systems-012.question: At the same symbol rate and the same average optical power, changing from QPSK to 16QAM raises the OSNR needed for the same error rate. What is the main reason?
choices: 16QAM has four times the symbol rate of QPSK, so the receiver bandwidth becomes four times wider and the noise power grows in proportion to the bandwidth
16QAM uses only 16 phases and not amplitude, so adjacent phases differ by only 22.5 degrees and it is more sensitive to noise
With more constellation points at the same average power, neighboring points are closer, so the same noise more easily makes one be mistaken for another
comm-systems-012.explanation: In the complex plane, QPSK has 4 points and 16QAM has 16 points on a 4×4 grid. At equal average power, the squared distance between neighboring points is 1/5 that of QPSK (10 log₁₀5 ≈ 7 dB), so under ideal conditions with only white Gaussian noise the SNR needed for the same error rate is about 7 dB higher (about 6.7 dB near an error rate of 10⁻³). The bits carried per symbol rise from 2 for QPSK to 4, but in exchange the reach becomes shorter. In this question the symbol rate is the same, so neither the signal bandwidth nor the noise bandwidth changes. 16QAM uses both amplitude and phase; it is PSK formats such as QPSK that use phase only.

comm-systems-013.question: Which correctly pairs the basic configuration of a digital coherent receiver with the information it obtains?
choices: No local oscillator is used; the phase of the signal and its two polarization components are read directly from the intensity detected by the square-law photodetector
The signal is mixed with a local oscillator in a 90° hybrid and detected with balanced photodetectors, giving the in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) field components for each polarization
The local oscillator must be locked optically to the phase of the signal (optical phase locking), and digital signal processing cannot handle phase, so only intensity is obtained
comm-systems-013.explanation: A photodetector output is proportional to the optical intensity |E|², so on its own it reveals nothing about phase. When a local oscillator (LO) at a nearby frequency is superimposed on the signal, the interference term carries the signal amplitude and phase. A 90° hybrid produces two sets of interference with the LO phase shifted by 0 and π/2, and balanced photodetectors cancel the LO's own intensity, giving I and Q; doing this for two polarizations gives 4 outputs. Optical phase locking was once needed, but in digital receivers the frequency offset and phase fluctuations are estimated and removed by signal processing after A/D conversion, so the phase information can be demodulated without fixing the phase optically.

comm-systems-014.question: Why can the digital signal processing of a coherent receiver compensate chromatic dispersion accumulated over thousands of km?
choices: Chromatic dispersion is a linear change that only adds a phase to each frequency component, so once the field amplitude and phase are known, a filter applying the opposite phase restores it

Chromatic dispersion is a nonlinear change proportional to the optical intensity, so the waveform before dispersion can be uniquely calculated back from the received intensity waveform and optical power
Square-law detection by the photodetector erases phase information, so the effect of dispersion, which appears as a phase shift, disappears along with it and needs no compensation
comm-systems-014.explanation: The change caused by chromatic dispersion only multiplies the field spectrum by a phase exp(jβ₂Lω²/2) that is proportional to the square of the angular frequency, leaving the amplitude unchanged. This is a linear all-pass filter, and multiplying by the opposite phase restores the original. A coherent receiver obtains the field (I and Q of two polarizations) as digital values, so a filter with the inverse characteristic matched to the distance compensates it, and adaptive filters also separate polarization rotation and polarization-mode dispersion. Direct detection, which measures only intensity, loses the phase, and the field before dispersion cannot be recovered uniquely from the intensity waveform. It is nonlinear effects such as self-phase modulation, not dispersion, that depend on intensity. Square-law detection erases the phase, while the waveform distorted by dispersion remains.

comm-systems-015.question: In long-haul WDM transmission, as the input power per channel is raised, the effective SNR at the receiver reaches a maximum and then falls. Which correctly explains why?
choices: Raising the input power degrades the EDFA noise figure, so ASE noise grows as the cube of the power and the SNR falls beyond a certain input power
Raising the input power increases the fiber loss coefficient (dB/km), so the received power levels off and the SNR against ASE noise falls beyond a certain point
The SNR against ASE noise improves in proportion to input power, but Kerr-effect nonlinear noise grows roughly as the cube of the power, so an optimum power balances the two
comm-systems-015.explanation: Amplifier ASE noise is nearly constant regardless of signal power, so raising the input power P improves the SNR against ASE in proportion to P. Meanwhile self-phase modulation, cross-phase modulation and four-wave mixing caused by the fiber Kerr effect behave like noise that disturbs the signal, with a magnitude roughly proportional to P³. The effective SNR takes the form P/(P_ASE + ηP³), so it peaks at the power where P_ASE = 2ηP³, and above that the nonlinear degradation wins. The EDFA noise figure is set mainly by the degree of population inversion and does not degrade as the cube of the input power. At these power levels the fiber loss coefficient is constant and does not depend on power.
